items.title: Lost photos from the heyday of punk and new wave
items.excerpt: Crash Bang — DB Burkeman’s latest photobook unearths photographs from his younger years as an aspiring music photographer, which sat undeveloped in his family home for decades. After his mother died, DB Burkeman return
items.content:
Crash Bang — DB Burkeman’s latest photobook unearths photographs from his younger years as an aspiring music photographer, which sat undeveloped in his family home for decades.

After his mother died, DB Burkeman returned to the family’s London home to clean out his childhood bedroom. There, he discovered a clear plastic bag filled with some 30 rolls of undeveloped black and white film – artefacts from his brief but wondrous stint as a rock & roll photographer at the turn of the 1980s. “I had thrown them into this drawer, thinking I’ll get to them later, but I was a bit of a mess,” Burkeman says. “The priority for me was never being a professional photographer. I would tell people that’s what I was doing, but the reality was [something else].”

Growing up in London during the ’70s, Burkeman remembers how stagnant youth culture had become, as he saw arena rock churning out a generation of clones. “Before ’76, everybody looked the same. It was just a sea of denim, right? It was just flared, flared jeans, jean jackets, and long hair,” he says. “Then all of a sudden there was this seismic shift where the Pistols had ripped a hole and changed the perception of what a rock band could be. There were 100 bands in London playing every night, and you only had to pay three quid, instead of £30, to see Eddie and the Hot Rods or the Damned. Everybody cut their hair and got rid of their flares. Everything just changed.”

Inspired, Burkeman dropped out of school at 16. Although he would later become a DJ, bringing jungle to New York in the ’90s, his musical talents lay dormant in his youth. But all was not lost. He explains, “I loved the image of the photographer; it’s almost like being a rock star. You were important, but you were also hiding behind, if not a guitar or drums, a camera.”

  • Read next: Riot grrrl is back. Do we need it more than ever?

But as a teen, business never came before pleasure, or quite frankly at all. “I knew I had a good eye, but I didn't have the people skills to really be able to pull it off,” Burkeman says. But that didn’t stop him from dreaming of becoming the next David Bailey or having a romp like David Hemmings in Blow-Up – only to discover reality is, indeed, the strangest fantasy of all. 

Although half of the film negatives had been lost to the ravages of time, the images that remained form an intoxicating portrait of the era. With the publication of Crash Bang: Pictures from a Punk (Blurring Books), Burkeman returns to where it all began: his years spent in London, New York, and Los Angeles between 1976 and 1982. 

  • Read next: Coming of age in New York’s ’70s punk heyday

As a budding rock photographer, Burkeman was the consummate insider, snapping scenes of musicians in their element. The Ramones rock out at the Rainbow and Alice Bag hangs out at home, while Sid Vicious and Nancy Spungen stride proudly out of Westminster Magistrate’s Court with their heads held high. Like many of his contemporaries, Burkeman developed a taste for heroin that eventually brought an end to his time on the scene. 

Today, the lost photographs fill a void in more ways than one. “I have a notoriously bad memory,” he says. “I did way too much acid between the ages of 14 and 16, and the psychiatrist told me that later in life, it would hurt my memory. I was like whatever, but sure enough he’s right.”

Crash Bang: Pictures from a Punk by DB Burkeman is published by Blurring Books.

items.title: Gold-tinged togetherness as Londoners flock to Primrose Hill for the solar eclipse
items.excerpt: Celestial gathering — Ella Glossop photographs the once in decades event from one the city’s most popular gathering spots, and the community spirit that encapsulated the moment. London hasn’t seen a solar eclipse this
items.content:
Celestial gathering — Ella Glossop photographs the once in decades event from one the city’s most popular gathering spots, and the community spirit that encapsulated the moment.

London hasn’t seen a solar eclipse this big since 1999.

Now in the big year or 2026, as thousands flock to the peak of Primrose Hill for the spectacle, there’s still something ’90s about it. Maybe it’s DIY-ness of all the tech: Meta glasses aren’t going to cut it here, so it’s holographic plastic lenses on cardboard straps. Phone cameras aren’t any good at picturing the sun, so people have brought different camera set ups, colanders, cereal-box projectors. Maybe it’s the fact that - during the day in summer - it’s not 35 degrees. Maybe, as the sun sets behind the moon and the light flattens, it’s the weird feeling that things might be okay.

A two-hour long affair – the eclipse reached its peak at 7:13PM, where over 90% of the sun is covered. We won’t see coverage this full again until 2081. The moment draws a big cheer from the crowd – who are huddled shoulder-to-shoulder on picnic rugs, with bottles of fizz popping and boom boxes pumping tunes. Then, as the sun emerges from behind the moon and normal daylight resumes, it’s hazy like it as at 5am.

  • Read next: Danny León pulls huge aerial in line with the solar eclipse

The modern world is fraught, big tech is big, the internet is loud – and once every few decades, we get a cosmic-sanctioned dose of perspective.

Huck’s Ella Glossop was there to capture the scenes. See her photographs below.

items.title: Surveying community and resistance in LGBTQ+ nightlife
items.excerpt: Sex, Clubs Dissent — A new book collates queer nightlife photography over the past 50 years, and the people who found refuge and safe spaces after dark. For over a century, queer nightlife thrived in the margins of soc
items.content:
Sex, Clubs Dissent — A new book collates queer nightlife photography over the past 50 years, and the people who found refuge and safe spaces after dark.

For over a century, queer nightlife thrived in the margins of society, driven underground by the criminalisation of sexuality and genders beyond the binary. Here in bars, clubs, ballrooms, warehouses, bathhouses, dungeons, cruising grounds, and strolls where sex is sold, generations have come together as an act of love and resistance against a world that shunned them. In those clandestine spaces, queer culture took root, becoming the lingua franca of music, style, beauty, glamour, and attitude – to say nothing of political activism and mutual aid that has saved lives and changed laws. 

Progress, however, can be a double-edged sword with the price of conditional freedom being cultural appropriation by a mainstream all too willing to erase the source. Ballroom colloquialisms like ‘the tea’, ‘kiki’, ‘shade’, ‘slay’, ‘reading’, ‘gagging’, and ‘giving’ are often mislabelled as ‘gen Z slang’ while contemporary and historic Black, brown and LGBTQ+ creators are paid dust. 

“There’s an acceleration of ubiquitous hyper capitalism and absorption of queer culture,” says author Amelia Abraham, on the phone from the streets of London. She’s just had a pop into The Photographers’ Gallery Bookshop, where her latest book, Sex, Clubs, Dissent: Visualising Queer Nightlife (MACK), is set among the new arrivals. The book’s red cover beckons with a keyhole glimpse of unbridled amour, revealed to be Meryl Meisler’s photograph of two women on the floor of Les Mouches, a members-only queer nightclub on Manhattan’s west side in the late 1970s. It’s a delectable promise of things to come. 

  • Read next: Inside Parkuir: the art project queering sport, space and our bodies

In Sex, Clubs, Dissent, Abraham explores the intersections of community, creativity, desire, and liberation, spotlighting the originators and innovators who blazed their own paths over half a century. Bringing together the work of artists including David Wojnarowicz, Sunil Gupta, Mariette Pathy Allen, Bruce LaBruce, Reynaldo Rivera, Linda Simpson, Lyle Ashton Harris, Clifford Prince King, and Chloe Sherman, the book is a panoramic landscape of the power and pride that’s only found when the night comes alive. 

Although Abraham started clubbing as a teen, it wasn’t until she discovered The Joiners Arms at the age of 21 that she finally had a place to call her own. “It was really chaotic. The floor was sticky with beer, the toilets were flooded, and it felt lawless and exciting to me,” she remembers fondly of the fabled Shoreditch dive bar. “It was loads of people from different subcultures coming together, a real melting pot, like the 60-year-old trans matriarch Stephanie, who always sat at the bar. It was one of the first places where I really fell in love with queer nightlife.” 

Drawn to the intergenerational aspect of Joiners, Abraham struck up a friendship with photographer Jeffrey Hinton, whose portrait of dancer Michael Clark, appears in the book. “Jeff is in his 60s and I’ve had the pleasure of hearing his stories about the nightlife that came before,” she says. “He has the same kind of attitude that Joiners had, which is quite DIY, egalitarian, and messy. That’s what we’re talking about with the word ‘dissent’ – a kind of disorderliness. Fuck it! Just do it – and do it for the love of it!” 

  • Read next: An intimate window into New York’s ’70s lesbian scene

It is this ethos that Abraham brings to the book, crafting a tour de force that is as much a photographic history as it is a family album, particularly in light of the criminalisation of queer sexuality around the globe. “The Gay Rights Movement started with visibility. Before that, the camera was dangerous,” she says. “Photographers from that time talk about how they couldn’t show their photos because someone might lose their job or their family. And that’s true for now for certain people.”

Sex, Clubs, Dissent: Visualising Queer Nightlife (2026) by Amelia Abraham published by MACK. It will have its US launch on September 8, 2026, at the Leslie-Lohman Museum of Art in New York.

items.title: In photos: Electric nights in ’70s Japan
items.excerpt: Tokyo–Koza — Keizō Kitajima’s new photobook explores the explosion of party culture of Tokyo and Okinawa during an era of rapid change in the country, as well as its stranger turns. Photography emerged at the vanguard
items.content:
Tokyo–Koza — Keizō Kitajima’s new photobook explores the explosion of party culture of Tokyo and Okinawa during an era of rapid change in the country, as well as its stranger turns.

Photography emerged at the vanguard in Japan as the 1968–69 university protests signified the rise of the New Left amid a global revolution against Western imperialism. Liberated from the myth of “objectivity” and false hierarchies of form, a small group of Japanese artists and critics including Daidō Moriyama and Nakahira Takuma came together to create Provoke, a photography magazine that embraced the raw, radical, and expressionistic possibilities of the medium. 

Although Provoke only ran three issues, its legacy would inspire generations of photographers from around the globe, beginning with native son, Keizō Kitajima. “I began photography in the mid-1970s, around the time when the political fervour symbolised by the May 1968 Paris Uprising was beginning to subside,” he says. “At that time, photography was considered one of the most cutting-edge and powerful means of expression in Japan, and I was deeply impressed by it.” 

Born in 1954 in Suzaka, Nagano Prefecture, Kitajima first discovered the work of Nobuyoshi Araki and Daidō Moriyama as a teen, going on to study with the latter in 1975 at WORK SHOP Photography School, founded by members of Provoke after the magazine folded. The two established a lifelong collaboration that took root the following year with the creation of CAMP, an artist-run gallery, darkroom, and meeting space in the Shinjuku district of Tokyo. 

With Moriyama’s support, Kitajima began exploring Koza, the historical name for Okinawa City and second largest city on the island following Tokyo. “Okinawa has numerous US military bases, and Koza is a nightlife district catering to American soldiers,” Kitajima says. “When I frequented Koza, it was shortly after the Vietnam War, and the town was bustling with many returning soldiers. People from all over Southeast Asia gathered in Koza to do business with the American soldiers. Many of them, including the soldiers, carried painful experiences in their hearts. I heard a thousand sad stories and a hundred happy stories from them.” 

With the recent publication of Keizo Kitajima: Tokyo–Koza (Little Big Man Books), the artist returns to the start of his career, retracing a fascinating chapter of Japanese photography and history. The lush, oversize paperback brings together Kitajima’s early works, Photographs of Okinawa (1975–1979) and Tokyo 1979, to create an electric portrait of Japanese nightlife during the second half of the decade. 

In 1979, Kitajima mounted a monthly series of exhibitions at CAMP showcasing black and white photographs made around the gallery in Shinjuku Ni-chome, a former red light district, accompanied by booklets titled Photo Express: Tokyo. “Japan was undergoing rapid urbanisation, and I was fascinated by the image and energy of the city,” he says. “The city seemed like a chaotic entity where light and darkness coexisted. Wandering through the labyrinthine alleys of Tokyo, I sought an encounter with a truth that transcended good and evil.” 

Kitajima remembers the experience as a whirlwind, excitedly photographing people who frequented the area, delighting when they would come to exhibition openings when their images were hung. “I attempted to compress the act of shooting, production, and exhibition into a single act, presenting it with maximum volume,” he says. Kitajima transformed CAMP into a darkroom by covering the walls with rolls of photographic paper, projecting the negatives onto them, developing them with a sponge, rinsing them in a bucket of water, and opening the show the very next day in that state. 

It is only now, half a century after these two series were made, that they can be seen together as Kitajima always dreamed. “For me, there are no past photographs. All the photographs I take, including street photography, are in the present tense and reflect my current position,” he says. “I believe it’s important to repeatedly revisit the same photographs, and I continue to re-examine the photographs I’ve taken, reinterpreting them in new contexts. My photographs are always beyond me.”

Keizo Kitajima: Tokyo–Koza is published by Little Big Man Books.

items.title: Defiance and pride in Chicano Camera Culture
items.excerpt: A Photographic History — A new major exhibition surveys Mexican American photography over six decades, platforming Chicano artists at a Chicano museum for the first time. Skyrocketing to fame in the late 1970s, comedia
items.content:
A Photographic History — A new major exhibition surveys Mexican American photography over six decades, platforming Chicano artists at a Chicano museum for the first time.

Skyrocketing to fame in the late 1970s, comedian Cheech Marin parlayed his position as one half of beloved stoner duo Cheech & Chong to become one of the world’s leading proponents of Chicano (Mexican American) art. In 2022, the Cheech Marin Center for Chicano Art & Culture, aka The Cheech, opened its doors, making history as the first museum devoted exclusively to “all things Chicano art”.

Hailing from Los Angeles, curator Elizabeth Ferrer remembers the museum’s opening as an important event, both for the community and for herself. Recognising she was among like minds, she set forth to create Chicano Camera Culture: A Photographic History, 1966-2026, an epic celebration of Chicano life as seen through 150 works across multiple generations now on view at the Cheech.

Featuring nearly 50 photographers including trailblazers Louis Carlos Bernal, George Rodriguez, and María Varela; innovators Reynaldo Rivera, Kathy Vargas, and Ken Gonzales-Day; and contemporary artists Guadalupe Rosales, Star Montana, and Thalía Gochez, Chicano Camera Culture forms a map of photographic history that has been largely disregarded by industry and institutions alike. 

  • Read next: Down and out in east LA: vintage shots of Chicano life

“The photographic record, whether from the viewpoint of photojournalists, documentarians, hobbyists, or artists, was created by the white gaze, and for a long time that fact was by and large taken for granted,” Ferrer says. “With the rise of the Civil Rights movement, the Chicano gaze comes into play. This means that for the first time, Chicanos are representing other Chicanos, typically, people who would otherwise be anonymous or unrecognised.” 

Like Ferrer’s 2021 book, Latinx Photography in the United States: A Visual History, Chicano Camera Culture is a landmark work, exploring Chicano photography as a cultural ethos born from knowledge of self. Rather than ascribe descriptors to identity, Ferrer maps its expression across generations, exploring the age-old questions of the human condition with a tender heart and a knowing eye. 

“All of the work in the show illuminates in one way or another, what it means to be Chicano,” she says. “Many of the themes addressed by the photographers – pride in identity, our struggle for agency and autonomy, the values we place in family and home, and the ways we create and claim space – are unsurprising. But what is impressive is the innovative ways in which they have been elaborated.” 

  • Read next: Vibrant photos of L.A.’s contemporary lowrider culture

Organised around themes of self/portraiture, domestic life, protests, border stories, and alternate realities, Chicano Camera Culture is a magnificent archive of collective resistance against an occupying force that has vilified and criminalised indigenous and mestizo communities, while telling the stories of the people and their cultures.

“From the beginning, the Chicano gaze has been about expressing pride in Chicano identity, preserving our history, uplifting cultural and spiritual values, validating persons out of the mainstream, and giving visibility to members of our own community,” Ferrer says. “As for what it means to tell Chicano stories by Chicano artists in a Chicano museum in the United States in 2026, I’d say it’s high time!” 

Chicano Camera Culture: A Photographic History, 1966–2026 is on view through September 6, 2026, at the Cheech Marin Art Center in Riverside, California. The catalogue is distributed by the Washington University Press for the Riverside Art Museum.

items.title: Grainy, yearning memories of Europe’s ’90s free rave heyday
items.excerpt: Never Alone — A new photobook from Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi presents pictures they made over seven years while touring the continent as part of the Tekno Mobil Squad soundsystem crew. It archives parties, people and a li
items.content:
Never Alone — A new photobook from Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi presents pictures they made over seven years while touring the continent as part of the Tekno Mobil Squad soundsystem crew. It archives parties, people and a lifestyle largely consigned to the past.

In 1994, the British government led by John Major passed the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act. It criminalised unlicensed raves, making it illegal for 20 or more people to gather and listen to “sounds wholly or predominantly characterised by the emission of a succession of repetitive beats”.

At the time, UK free party culture had reached its zenith. Crews such as DiY, Spiral Tribe and Circus Warp were organising raves across common land and abandoned buildings around the country, culminating in the 1992 Castlemorton Common rave that attracted tens of thousands of people across the weekend.

Without charging money for entry, and consciously making use of public and dilapidated spaces, free party culture was idealistic and egalitarian. But now faced with the prospect of up to three months in prison for attending or organising raves, some felt that the UK no longer offered the opportunity for them to live the nomadic, free lifestyles that they dreamed of.

  • Read next: Sepia splashed memories of Britain’s ’90s squatting and free party scene

Crews such as Spiral Tribe and Bedlam followed in the footsteps of the Mutoid Waste Company in the late ’80s, setting off across Europe with no end goal, organising parties as they travelled eastwards through France, Germany, the Czech Republic, Italy and beyond. Inspired by the parties and culture, homegrown European crews began popping up and organising their own versions of raves, or “Teknivals” as they were often referred to. 

In 1997, Italian photographers Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi stumbled across their first raves. Both were grew up around Milan and attended the same high school, with Clementi’s parents being involved in the post-hippie and punk movements of the late ’70s and ’80s. Her first rave was on the ex-Breda industrial lands – formerly a huge factory where trains were built. “I first encountered free parties and rave culture around 1997,” Clementi says. “From that moment on, I immediately felt that this was where I belonged.”

Morandi, meanwhile, attended her first in an abandoned factory in Bologna. “I experienced absolute freedom and immediately knew I had found something unique,” she remembers. 

  • Read next: As Italy’s rave culture faces crackdowns, a cyberpunk citadel fights to survive

They both instantly got the bug, as people in the UK had at the beginning of the decade, and similarly-minded rebellious folks across Europe did too. That same year, they founded the Tekno Mobil Squad along with a group of friends, and for the best part of the next decade, Clementi and Morandi travelled Europe, moving beyond Italy’s borders while throwing raves and teknivals in “abandoned factories, former military sites, forests, beaches and open countryside”.

Their new photobook Never Alone: 1997-2004 Raving in Europe, documents the crew’s heyday between 1997 and 2004, filled with nostalgic, black-and-white shots of the time that are part-diaristic and part-documentation of a culture that existed largely hidden away on the fringes of mainstream society. Without their pictures, the time would likely have been consigned to memory.

Clementi and Morandi would take pictures often for no real reason beyond cherishing moments. “We loved photography,” they explain. “At the time, we weren’t consciously documenting history – we were just photographing our lives. Since photography was entirely analogue, very few people were doing it. There was no pressure to document every experience. Every frame mattered. Photographs were memories, not content for social media.”

  • Read next: As Hanoi’s nightlife faces raids & repression, its underground scene modulates

There’s shots of raves in full flow, with huge soundsystems, packed crowds, and DJs spinning techno, acid, jungle, drum & bass and more to dancers, but it’s also the books quieter moments that shine the brightest. Intimate portraits of their friends and pets in their trucks are interspersed with moments relaxing in nature or lying on top of soundsystems. 

The pictures showcase genuine community among the travelling troupe, who moved around Europe in search of nothing but parties, music, creativity and freedom. “We lived on four wheels. The trucks were our homes and carried the soundsystems,” Clementi and Morandi say. “Every weekend we searched for a new location, spreading the word through flyers and word of mouth.” 

Run ins with police were also documented. Different countries and municipalities saw a wide range in responses to their parties. “[We had police encounters] many times,” they explain. “Sometimes they confiscated our trucks or shut down parties. Other times they escorted us to safer locations.”

  • Read next: We took techno legend Chris Liberator to a virtual rave, here’s what went down

As free party culture grew in popularity, and became commercialised into the global festival and nightclub circuit we know today, the images capture the lightning in a bottle moment of the ’90s, in the early, radical days of the movement, before authorities had time to properly organise and legislate to curb it.

The project then, serves as a reminder of a bygone era. “We realised we had a unique archive documenting one of Europe’s most significant underground movements and wanted to turn it into cultural memory,” Morandi and Clementi say. “It is visual memory, freedom, art and hope – a project that tells the story of many lives.”

Never Alone: 1997-2004 Raving in Europe by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi is published by Propaganda / Drago.

items.title: Queer resistance & sun-soaked solidarity at the world’s largest trans pride march
items.excerpt: Our Future, Our Fight — Over the weekend, over 150,000 people marched at the London Trans+ Pride, with the parade ending at Trafalgar Square for the first time in history. On Saturday, the streets of central London bec
items.content:
Our Future, Our Fight — Over the weekend, over 150,000 people marched at the London Trans+ Pride, with the parade ending at Trafalgar Square for the first time in history.

On Saturday, the streets of central London became a sea of colour, resistance and celebration as an estimated 150,000 people joined London Trans+ Pride – making it the largest trans pride march in the world.

Now in its sixth year, the march arrives at a moment of heightened political pressure for trans people in the UK. Organisers described 2026 as the “most politically urgent year” in the event’s history, with this year’s theme – Our Future, Our Fight – reflecting a growing sense of determination in the face of escalating public debate and policy changes affecting trans rights.

Ending in Trafalgar Square for the first time in history, many placards focus on the basic humanity of trans people – a response to the disproportionate fearmongering and attention aimed at trans people in the media. Messages reading “We are all human” and “Why are you so obsessed with me?” try to restore a little perspective. One attendee carries a frame simply reading “look closer, it’s just people” – a poignant point when it’s a group of smiling, glitter-clad marchers waving pink flags behind it. 

  • Read next: Euphoric portraits of queer joy and resistance at Trans Pride Brighton

The message took on a painful new resonance just hours later, when news emerged of a terrorist attack on a Pride event in Berlin on the night after London Trans+ Pride. Organisers acknowledged that the news “may feel particularly frightening or overwhelming” coming so soon after the event.

“We will not allow violence to isolate us or take away our right to gather, protest, celebrate and live freely,” they wrote in a statement on Instagram.

“We also reject any attempt by the far right to exploit this tragedy to fuel Islamophobia, racism or further division.”

Inspired by Trans Pride Brighton – the first ever trans-specific Pride event in the UK – the London march has grown dramatically since it first drew 1,500 people in 2019. “We thought things were going to get better and better. It got to 2015, 2016 and things started to go backwards,” Brighton Trans Pride cofounder Fox Fisher tells Huck. According to the ILGA Rainbow Map – which ranks and measures European countries based on their laws and policies that affect LGBTQ+ folk – in 2026 the UK was the 22nd best country to live in for queer people out of 49. In 2015, the UK was ranked first.

  • Read next: In photos: Euphoric joy at the UK’s biggest ever anti-racism march

Instagram

Create an account or log in to Instagram - Share what you're into with the people who get you.

www.instagram.com

“To have an event like Trans Pride in London, where we’re saying ‘these are our streets’ – it’s so important,” Fisher continues. “To be able to look after each other, have a safety net when the other safety nets have been pulled away from us.”

For broadcaster and podcaster Jack Remmington, the march was a chance to push back against the idea that opposition to trans people represents the public mood. “The opposition to trans people is a powerful but very small vocal minority,” he tells Huck. “It’s days like today that show the love and unity, and hopefully show trans people that there are so many people that are on their side and that love them. My life would be noticeably so much less enriched without trans people in it.”

As the march grows in size year on year, it also feels increasingly charged – with the characteristic prideful eccentricity and joy cutting through a palpable sense of fear felt by many in the community. Cars honk as they went past, people high up in shop windows show their support. Music blares from boom boxes on rollers, drums and trombones. This is a loud, visible reminder that is urgently needed – that on these streets, trans people do not have to face this moment alone.

Huck’s Ella Glossop was there to capture the day.

  • Read next: Revisiting Casa Susanna, the legendary Trans refuge in pre-Stonewall America

items.title: In photos: Black Texas life since emancipation
items.excerpt: Kinship & Community — A new photobook and exhibition showcases the rich culture, history and community of African American folks in the Lone Star State, whose existence in the region predates colonial Britain. On J
items.content:
Kinship & Community — A new photobook and exhibition showcases the rich culture, history and community of African American folks in the Lone Star State, whose existence in the region predates colonial Britain.

On June 19, 1865 – some months after the Confederacy surrendered in ignominious defeat – Black folks in Texas were liberated from the bondage of chattel slavery. A year later, the first celebration of Jubilee Day (later Juneteenth) was held, the annual event to help people register to vote. During the first flush of Reconstruction, Black communities built Freedmen’s towns, forming the heart and soul of newly emerging cities like Houston with its fabled Third and Fourth Wards. 

By the 1870s, photography had democratised the portrait, wresting the power of representation from the powerbrokers and restoring it to the people themselves. Inexpensive image making techniques, such as tintypes and crayon portraits, became popular among Black folks on both sides of the camera. But it wasn’t until 1995, when writer and filmmaker Alan Govenar and artist Kaleta Doolin teamed up to create the Texas African American Photography Archive (TAAP) that this history could be told in full. Home to 60,000 images made between the 1850s and the 1970s in a broad array of formats, TAAP has become one of the foremost repositories of work by Black photographers in the world. 

With the new exhibition and book, Kinship & Community: Selections from the Texas African American Photography Archive (Aperture/Documentary Arts), co-curators Nicole R. Fleetwood and Brian Wallis craft a panoramic landscape of everyday life as seen from the inside looking out. Featuring work by Earlie Hudnall Jr., Marion Butts, Elnora W. Frazier, Alonzo Jordan, and Benny A. Joseph, as well as a photographic essay by Rahim Fortune, and essay by Deborah Willis, Kinship & Community is a celebration of Black Texas in all its multi-splendored glory. 

  • Read next: ‘Hyper-American’ photos of life in rural Texas

“Texans are very proud of their history, but I think the rest of the country, and maybe even the world, has reduced and misread the history of Black Texas,” says Fleetwood, who has her own personal ties to the state. Hailing from a small town in Ohio, she moved to Houston briefly when her mother remarried but was completely overwhelmed. “I left after a year,” she says. “I didn’t understand the landscape of Texas.” 

But Fleetwood, who is now based in New York, has come full circle and has a place in Houston to which she regularly returns. She, like many of her generation, have embraced remigration, returning to the South and finding kinship and community among new arrivals from Nigeria and Black Americans who never left. Personal engagement is a hallmark of Fleetwood’s work, from her landmark 2020 exhibition and book, Marking Time: Art in the Age of Mass Incarceration, to her forthcoming memoir, Between the River and the Railroad Tracks. 

  • Read next: A visual journey through Texas during lockdown

Seen through the lens of TAAP, the rich cultural histories of Black Texas form a majestic tapestry of everyday life. Fleetwood points to the cowboy, originally a radicalised term used to diminish the contributions of Black cowhands, as well as the presence of Black communities that predate Jamestown, the first British settlement on the continent. “The earliest African presence in Texas were people who [were brought by Spanish colonisers] before the formation of the US as a nation state, and many of them were early settlers in rural parts of Texas,” she says. 

With roots that run deeper than the nation itself, Black Texas is the cornerstone of America. “The sense of pride in Texas is unlike any other state,” Fleetwood says. “One of my brothers was born there and he is so Texan. He lives in a community in Houston called Hiram Park, and it’s home to Black cowboys that Rahim Fortune has been documenting. If you’re hanging out in my brother’s yard, you’ll see five or 10 guys riding their horses and playing music. They’re somewhat country, somewhat hip hop, and it just blows my mind.’”

  • Read next: Rahim Fortune’s dreamlike vision of the Black American South

Kinship & Community: Selections from the Texas African American Photography Archive and Rahim Fortune - Between a Memory and Me: A Photographic Essay are on view through September 5, 2026, at Art + Practice in collaboration with the California African Art Museum in Los Angeles. Kinship & Community is published by Aperture/Documentary Arts.

items.title: Youthful joy & end-of-era poignancy at a London school prom
items.excerpt: Leavers — For several years, Lewis Khan documented young people as they celebrated the last of their school days and the completion of their exams. The series is now collated in a new self-published photobook and short film.
items.content:
Leavers — For several years, Lewis Khan documented young people as they celebrated the last of their school days and the completion of their exams. The series is now collated in a new self-published photobook and short film.

The protagonists of Lewis Khan’s Leavers revel in a cloak of youth-shaped exuberance. Draped in sequins and silk or adorned with a bowtie and sunglasses – one teenager wears a sash pronouncing him ‘Prom King’, others don the traditional dress of their home lives – these young people appear confident, oftentimes euphoric and occasionally serious (but ultimately comfortable), embracing the kind of party atmosphere uniquely fuelled by exams being over. A soft glow, courtesy of the photographer’s preferred use of medium format and Super 8, underscores the gravity of the moment, between the end of school and what comes next. “It’s a moment of joy and celebration,” reflects Khan. 

The near-decade long project first took shape, loosely, in July 2017 when the photographer accompanied his mum on a night time stroll around their neighbourhood in Vauxhall, south London. It was the type of local walk that doesn’t entertain any real objective, recalls Khan, “No direction, just soaking things up.” At some point they noticed groups of teenagers spilling out of a nearby school: their shiny suits and glittering frocks generating a spectacle in an otherwise grey landscape of concrete and traffic. His interest piqued, Khan reached out to the school via a friend’s mum who taught there, and arranged to shoot the following year’s event.

Despite its popularity in the UK growing substantially in the past few decades, prom remains largely an American phenomenon for many, witnessed predominantly through TV and film, where the lead characters are generally white and typically depicted as middle or upper middle class. Khan, who grew up in the area, doesn’t recall his own secondary school ever hosting a prom. “I don’t think it had the resources,” he says. “I would have gone to it though. And if my old school ever does do a prom, I would love to photograph it.” In his work however, there’s a sense of familiarity about the occasion; a recognisable intimacy that betrays the specificity of the scene. Now, following an exhibition at 1014 gallery in Dalston earlier this year, the photographer has self-published a book of his prom pictures. 

  • Read next: Inside the bedrooms of American youth during the ’80s and ’90s

Beyond the project’s strong visual component, there’s an important social factor and a cultural significance that Khan observed early on, which quickly became a central motivation for returning every year. “I’ve grown up knowing teenagers to be treated with suspicion and contempt,” he shares, referencing the ASBO era. Entering his teens in the early 2000s, the photographer remembers well the controversy of anti-social behaviour orders, which arrived with Tony Blair’s Labour government in 1998 – introduced as part of the Crime and Disorder Act – and how they coincided with a culture of councils rescinding resources like youth clubs for teenagers. “At the same time, they were installing high frequency audio signals in public places that only younger people could hear, making those spaces inhospitable.

“It created this sense that young people weren’t to be supported or understood, but managed and moved on,” he continues. “Those attitudes were often mapped onto existing social and racial inequalities, which you can see reflected in patterns of systemic racism, for example police stop and search figures in areas like Lambeth [where the school is], which disproportionately affect Black boys and men.” Leavers then, becomes a counternarrative, challenging negative stereotypes perpetuated by biased newspaper headlines. As Khan observes, “The prom felt like a beautiful antidote. A space of self-worth and pride.” 

In his photographs, made with a pronounced sense of care, Khan reframes both what a prom can look like and how teenagers from inner-city London state schools are perceived; the scenes are joyful and the environment feels kind, as friends and classmates dance, joke, and encourage one another. There is a sense that judgement – both the sort presented in classic teen movies with high-stakes proms, and the kind found in ‘only three school children at a time’ signs in London corner shops – has been removed for a night.

  • Read next: Unseen portraits of high school teenagers in ’70s New York

This sentiment is amplified in an accompanying short film, made in 2022, which features a specially-written poem by former Young People’s Laureate Caleb Femi, who grew up in Peckham in the neighbouring borough of Southwark. With Glass, which Femi recites alongside Lara George’s ‘Dansaki’, his words affect a kinship with the young people in Khan’s images, further sharpening the context in which they celebrate and the significance of their coming together; elsewhere a teacher makes this feeling explicit, tenderly announcing: “The most important thing is, through it all, you have made it to today. Whatever you went through – whatever you didn’t go through – somehow you are here today, and that is a celebration.”

Prior to Khan’s Dalston show, which marked his first solo exhibition, in spring last year Khan presented Leavers at photo festival Peckham24, while in September it travelled to Poland as part of Night of Photography with the Museum of Warsaw. “The response has been really generous,” he says today. “What’s stood out is how people connect – in Peckham there’s a familiarity with it being local, but even in places like Poland people still relate through their own memories of youth and moments of transition. That’s probably been the biggest surprise – how universal those feelings are, despite the work being so rooted in a specific place.”

  • Read next: “A party is a microcosm of a nation”: Caleb Femi on the decline of the house party

Leavers by Lewis Khan is available to purchase via his official website.

items.title: Harry Gruyaert’s vintage, kaleidoscopic scenes of New York
items.excerpt: A Sense of Place — For 50 years, the Belgian photographer and Magnum Photos member has been capturing NYC’s colourful chaos. A new photobook and exhibition showcase his unique, technicolour view of the city. In 1968, B
items.content:
A Sense of Place — For 50 years, the Belgian photographer and Magnum Photos member has been capturing NYC’s colourful chaos. A new photobook and exhibition showcase his unique, technicolour view of the city.

In 1968, Belgian photographer Harry Gruyaert received an offer he could not refuse: a chance to photograph on the set of François Reichenbach’s new film set in New York City. He made the journey by boat and remembers seeing the Statue of Liberty as it sailed into the harbour.

Gruyaert stayed with dancer Trisha Brown at her downtown loft back when Soho was awash with abandoned industrial buildings with crumbling facades. Brown’s building, 80 Wooster Street, was one of the neighbourhood’s first artists’ co-op, home to Fluxus Art movement founder George Maciunas and avant-garde filmmaker Jonas Mekas, who opened Cinematheque I on the ground floor to screen experimental films. It was a sign of things to come. 

“When I arrived in Soho, there were no restaurants, no galleries, no nothing. To go to a lively place, you had to go up to Washington Square,” Gruyaert says. That suited him just fine. New York’s chaotic energy was overwhelming and intoxicating in equal parts, standing in radical contrast to the dull grey of Belgium. He took to the streets, photographing the city with fresh eyes, crafting kaleidoscopic images of daily life on luminous Kodachrome film. 

  • Read next: In Photos: A decade growing up in pre-gentrification Lower East Side

On that same visit, Gruyaert discovered Pop Art, the quintessentially American meditation on mass culture that blurred the boundaries between high and low art. “What interested me were people like Robert Rauschenberg who were using all kinds of elements you found on the street,” he says. “There was a certain vulgarity of advertising, which in Europe was not used very much in art. It gave something new and very contemporary.” 

Over the next half century, Gruyaert would return to New York, time and again, amassing an extraordinary archive of images that capture the freewheeling spirit of city life. With the publication of Harry Gruyaert: New York (Thames & Hudson), Gruyaert brings the city to us. The large-format book weaves together the photographer’s hypnotic scenes with fictional vignettes by filmmaker Cédric Klapisch. 

“Flicking through the pages of this book gives you the same feeling you’d get walking down a New York street,” Klapisch writes. “You’re not following a thread of logic, but you can feel an effervescence, a commotion, a frenetic fusion of people, signs, street furniture, advertising, and cars…. When I look at [Harry’s] photos, I immediately see life. I often find myself wondering who these people are that I’m looking at; they turn into characters in a potential movie.”

  • Read next: When the Chelsea Hotel was New York’s countercultural epicentre

Gruyaert, who joined Magnum Photos in 1982, does not consider himself a journalist and had given little thought to people in his pictures until reading Klapisch’s vivid portraits of their inner lives. For Gruyaert, people are but one element of street, rather than the central focus of his work. Drawing inspiration from Magnum Photos co-founder, Henri Cartier-Bresson, he explains, “The genius of [his work] is that it is not only well composed, but that it says a lot of things about the place and the time it was shot, so that the different layers gives certain depth to the photographs.” 

It is this sense of place that forms the heart and soul of Gruyaert’s work, whether walking the streets of New York, Paris, Antwerp, Moscow, Mumbai, Zanzibar, and Tokyo. Taken together, they can be seen in the new exhibition, Harry Gruyaert: A Sense of Place, during Les Rencontres d’Arles.

Harry Gruyaert: A Sense of Place is on view July 6 – October 4, 2026, at Chapelle Saint-Martin du Méjan during Les Rencontres d’Arles in Arles, France.

Harry Gruyaert: New York is published by Thames & Hudson.
